comments.author: @JohnDlugosz
comments.text:
Re coding:  I gave ChatGPT 4o one of the problems from Mind Your Decisions (the one about averaging the house numbers and finding the person's age) and it generated math equations about the problem but could not figure it out.  It wrote code to brute-force the answer, but it did not find one.  The code ran just fine; it just wasn't exactly right to model the problem.  Reading through it, it appears to be a faithful translation of the stated problem.
That's one issue with coding proficiency.  Writing good/correct code doesn't mean anything if the underlying engineering is wrong.

Anyway, I gave the same problem to 4o1-preview (without the OCR since file upload is not exposed for that model) and it crushed it, solving the problem using number theory.  Then I asked what was wrong with the code, just pasting the whole file into the prompt.  It took a few seconds, and explained several mistakes, corrected them, and demonstrated that it then found the answer.

comments.text:
The ONE thing you can know about someone talking about AI is when they say "the bigger the model, the better", which is completely untrue.
It is the same as saying "the fullest the bottle of a beverage is, the better the beverage". A model is not the data it draws upon. Lets say you have a Recurrent model, a Convolution Model, and a Transformer Model. You can have a Recurrent model with a WEIGHT data of 300G, the transformer model of 7G will be better. Not only that, but if the 300G of weights is meaningless, and the 7G is of well mapped data, the 7G is better. Throughout the video, the host makes a lot of assumptions taking the misconceptions of popular notions into account. To have an idea, imagine that you have 14 cubes to choose from, and another person has 8 cubes to choose from. You are tasked to form the more words the faster, but the 10 cubes you have are only consonants, and the 10 cubes the other person has has vowels and consonants. Furthermore, you are tasked to form words in your own languages, and you speak Turkish, the other person speaks English, which has simpler and more similar words. And that is the general tone of all these AI videos on the Internet. If you dont believe me, ask Mr GPT itself, and it will tell you as much.

comments.author: @Me__Myself__and__I
comments.text:
I missed that previous "rise of the software engineers" discussion you mentioned.  As someone extremely experienced in this field I'll answer: no.  First lets clarify that coder, programmer, developer and software engineer are all functionally the same.  Same skillset, just different term/title.  I've been called all 4 many times.  

If things do go in this direction the reason the anser is "no" is because a different but related skillset already exists that would fill this role: the Software Architect.  Most developers are not good at software architecture, because it is a different set of skills that are more important at the big picture scope.  In fairness most good architects aren't good developers.  Its rare to find someone who is good at both.  Anyway, I expect architects will likely be the last to get repaced by AI because they will probably be the last humans orchestrating things before software becomes fully automated.
